Photo location guide

How to geotag photos with a timed GPX track on Mac

Last updated November 5, 2026

Have a recorded GPX track and camera photos from the same outing? This guide focuses on track coverage and camera time, then reviewing the match on Mac. For Apple Watch workouts, LensPin on iPhone or iPad can read routes directly from Apple Health without a GPX export.

A usable GPX track needs both coordinates and times from the actual outing. Check those first, then match camera times and review the proposed locations.

Check that you have the right kind of GPX

A GPX file is a container for geographic information. For matching photos by capture time, you need recorded points that associate a time with a location. A planned walking route can look exactly right on a map while containing no record of when you were at each point. It cannot establish where a photograph belongs at a particular moment.

  1. Find the recording from the same outing as the photos, rather than a route planned for a future trip.
  2. Check the start and end times against your shooting period.
  3. Look for gaps, pauses or sections that belong to a different day.
  4. Keep an untouched copy of the track while you investigate any time mismatch.

GPX can come from a phone recording app, a GPS recorder or a watch service that offers an activity-track export. Export availability varies, so consult the service you actually used. The site’s guide to getting a GPX file is a useful starting point. LensPin does not record GPX itself.

Understand what matching by time can establish

The camera photo supplies a capture time; the track supplies recorded locations over time. A matching workflow uses that relationship to propose a position. Matching uses your recorded movements; it does not identify landmarks in the image. A track recorded by someone else helps only if that person was actually with you at the relevant time.

Even a genuine recording can be incomplete. If you stopped recording during a transfer, a later photo may fall outside the covered period. If the recorder stayed in a car while you walked away, its position is not your shooting position. Check what the device was doing before trusting the line on the map.

Resolve the camera clock offset first

Choose a camera photo taken at a recognizable place on the track. Compare its displayed capture time with the time you were actually there. Check another reference photo later in the outing. If both are displaced similarly, a clock or time-zone difference may explain the mismatch.

For example, a camera left on home time can be hours away from a phone using local time. This is an example of a possible error, not a reason to apply a fixed offset to every trip. Check the date around midnight and any daylight-saving change. GPX timestamps may use UTC, so compare actual moments rather than assuming identical displayed hours mean identical times.

If you reset a camera clock during the trip, work on the periods separately. Different camera bodies can need different corrections. Avoid editing all capture dates as an experiment: first use a matching preview and verify the direction of the correction with a known location.

Prepare the photos in Apple Photos on Mac

Put the photos in Apple Photos before matching; LensPin does not work on arbitrary Finder folders. Use a Mac Smart Album to identify photos without GPS. If you simply remember one place, use the built-in Info-window method instead.

Review a GPX batch with LensPin for Mac

LensPin offers four sources: geotagged iPhone photos from the same trip; geotagged photos from other GPS-equipped cameras; GPX tracks; Apple Health workout routes. On Mac, use reference photos or GPX; read Health workout routes on iPhone or iPad. Journeys are grouped automatically, and processing happens on device.

  1. Choose a small camera-photo batch without locations and the track covering that period.
  2. Preview any camera clock offset you established. The preview does not change capture dates.
  3. Review every suggested location before saving. Check the beginning and end, long pauses and any point where your route doubles back.
  4. Skip suggestions outside reliable coverage or at places contradicted by the photograph.
  5. Save the reviewed suggestions and reopen those photos in Apple Photos to check the resulting maps.

Existing locations are never overwritten. If an image already has a wrong pin, correct it separately in Photos. A successful save means the library accepted the location; it does not prove the track or clock assumption was accurate. Keep that distinction when checking the result.

Check exports separately from the library

LensPin saves to the Apple Photos library, not the original camera files. If you also need GPS inside a standalone image, export a JPG copy with Include location enabled. Inspect the copy’s GPS before sharing; the GPX track and the geotagged image can both reveal private places.
